name: Four Violins
editorial_article: "Four Violins" is a seminal work by experimental composer Tony Conrad, composed in 1964. A cornerstone of the American minimalist movement, the piece reflects Conrad's deep-seated fascination with just intonation, the physics of sound, and the rejection of 19th-century bravura performance traditions. By applying specific, drone-based modal tunings to four string instruments, Conrad sought to create a sonic environment where the focus shifted from melodic progression to the physical resonance of the instruments themselves. The work functions as a study in sustained sound and microtonal harmony, stripping away the traditional narrative of western music in favor of a visceral, immersive experience.\n\nEmerging from the same circle of Downtown New York avant-garde practitioners as La Monte Young and Marian Zazeela—the so-called "Dream Music" collective—Conrad developed "Four Violins" during a period when he was actively questioning the role of the performer and the nature of composition. Influenced by his study of early 17th-century violin techniques, which he perceived as being more akin to folk or "bluegrass" fiddling than to the vibrato-heavy, expressive styles of the classical era, Conrad focused on the purity of the sound produced by long-held, precisely tuned notes. The result is a piece that predates much of the "minimalist" canon, offering a radical alternative to the dominant compositional paradigms of the era. It remains a vital document for those interested in the history of drone music and the evolution of experimental string performance.
